procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Gujarat High Court dated October 23, 1969, dismissing in limine Criminal Revision No. 407 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The appellant filed a writ petition challenging the imposition of a fine, which was rejected on August 25, 1969.
2. The appellant filed a criminal revision against the order of the Sessions Judge, which was dismissed in limine by a single Judge (Shelat J.) of the Gujarat High Court on October 23, 1969.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the order of the Gujarat High Court. The appellant appeared in person. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: This appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant qualifies as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken for summary delivery of property.

facts: The appellant operated a tea stall and a refreshment stall at a railway station under two separate, identical agreements with the Railway administration.

The agreements were terminated, and the railway administration sought to repossess the stalls using a summary procedure under section 138 of the Indian Railways Act, which is applicable to 'railway servants'.
The appellant contested this, arguing he was not a railway servant.
law: The issue was determined by the definition of a 'railway servant' under section 3(7) read with section 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.
Section 138 of the Act allows for a summary remedy for the delivery of railway property detained by a railway servant whose service has been discharged.
application: The Court examined the terms of the agreements governing the parties.
It found that the agreements expressly reserved to the Railway administration "extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also of controlling the manner of doing the work."
The Court reasoned that this high degree of control was the decisive factor in classifying the appellant as a railway servant for the purposes of the Act.
The Court also noted that in the proceedings before it, the appellant did not actually dispute being a railway servant; rather, he argued from that position to claim other protections.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that because the terms of the agreements gave the Railway administration extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the appellant's work, he qualified as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act. Therefore, summary action for the delivery of property under section 138 could be legally taken against him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of the contract amounted to the appellant's 'discharge', thereby lawfully permitting the initiation of proceedings against him under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.

facts: The appellant ran two stalls at a railway station under agreements with the railway administration.
The agreements were terminated by the railway administration after the appellant committed certain irregularities and failed to pay a fine.
When the appellant did not vacate the stalls, the railway administration initiated proceedings under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act to secure possession.
law: Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act provides a summary remedy for the railway administration to recover property detained by a "discharged" railway servant.
The definition of a "railway servant" is found in Section 3(7) read with Section 148(2) of the Act.
application: The Supreme Court upheld the findings of the lower courts (the Magistrate and the Sessions Judge).
The Sessions Judge had explicitly held that the "termination of the contract amounted to the appellant's discharge."
The Supreme Court agreed that due to the extensive control the railway administration had over the appellant's work, he qualified as a "railway servant" under the Act.
By affirming the lower courts' decisions, the Supreme Court implicitly agreed that for the purposes of Section 138, the termination of the appellant's contract was equivalent to being "discharged."
The Court noted that as a discharged railway servant who refused to deliver the property, the appellant was subject to the summary proceedings under Section 138.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, effectively deciding that the termination of his contract did constitute a "discharge" as a railway servant, which lawfully permitted the railway administration to initiate summary repossession proceedings against him under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the relationship between the appellant and the railway administration was one of master and servant.

facts: The appellant operated two stalls (a tea stall and a refreshment stall) at a railway station under agreements with the railway administration.
The agreements stipulated that the appellant had to run the stalls in accordance with the directions of the railway administration.
law: The determination of a master-servant relationship is a question of fact that depends on the terms of the agreement as a whole.
A key characteristic of a master-servant relationship is the power of the master to direct, regulate, and control the manner in which the work is done.
The relevant legal definition was that of a "railway servant" under section 3(7) read with section 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.
application: The Court examined the terms of the agreements between the appellant and the railway administration.
It found that the agreements expressly gave the railway administration "extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also of controlling the manner of doing the work."
This high degree of control was deemed sufficient to establish a master-servant relationship.
The Court also noted that in the lower court, the appellant had not disputed being a railway servant and, in fact, had claimed his position was on par with other railway servants.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the relationship was one of master and servant because the terms of the governing agreements gave the railway administration extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the appellant's work.

issue.issue_text: Whether the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge suffered from any legal infirmity that would justify interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant's contracts to run tea and refreshment stalls were terminated by the railway administration.
The administration sought to repossess the stalls through a Magistrate under section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.
The appellant challenged this action, first before the Sessions Judge and then the High Court, but was unsuccessful in both courts.

The lower courts determined that the appellant was a "railway servant" under the Indian Railways Act, and therefore, summary dispossession proceedings under section 138 were lawful after his contract was terminated (which amounted to a "discharge").
The appellant also alleged that the Magistrate's order was malicious because it was passed just five days after the High Court dismissed a separate writ petition filed by him.
law: Article 136 of the Constitution grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to interfere with judgments of lower courts.
Sections 3(7) and 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act define who qualifies as a "railway servant".
Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act allows for the summary dispossession of a railway servant from railway property after they have been discharged.
application: The Supreme Court directly reviewed the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge to check for any legal errors.
It explicitly stated that it was "unable to find any legal infirmity" in the decisions of the lower courts.
The Court upheld the conclusion of the lower courts that the appellant was indeed a "railway servant" as defined by the Indian Railways Act, against whom action under section 138 could be taken.
The Court also dismissed the appellant's allegation of malice, stating there was "no warrant for this assumption" and that the timing of the Magistrate's order did not establish malice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge did not suffer from any legal infirmity that would justify its interference under Article 136 of the Constitution. Consequently, the appeal was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant qualifies as a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken for summary delivery of property.
appellant_arguments: The appellant denied that he was a railway servant.
respondent_arguments: The appellant is a railway servant by virtue of Sections 3(7) and 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act, and therefore proceedings for summary delivery of property could be lawfully initiated against him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination of the contract amounted to the appellant's 'discharge', thereby lawfully permitting the initiation of proceedings against him under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.
appellant_arguments: Even if he was considered a railway servant, he had not been validly discharged.
respondent_arguments: The termination of the contract amounted to the appellant's discharge, which lawfully permitted the initiation of proceedings against him under Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the relationship between the appellant and the railway administration was one of master and servant.
appellant_arguments: By reason of being a railway servant, a master-servant relationship existed, which entitled him to the constitutional protection afforded to Government servants under Article 311.
respondent_arguments: While the appellant was a 'railway servant' under the statutory definition for the limited purposes of the Indian Railways Act, this did not grant him the full status of a government servant in a master-servant relationship entitled to Article 311 protection.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge suffered from any legal infirmity that would justify interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The lower court orders were legally infirm because he was not a railway servant, was not validly discharged, and was wrongly denied the protection of Article 311.
The appellant also raised procedural grounds, requesting to summon witnesses, adjourn the hearing to engage a senior counsel, and refer the case to a Constitution Bench.
respondent_arguments: The conclusions of the lower courts were legally correct and there was no infirmity in their orders that would justify interference.

cases.principle: To support the conclusion that the appellant was a 'railway servant' as defined in the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken under s. 138 of that Act, based on the terms of the agreements which gave the Railway administration extensive control over the appellant's work.

cases.case_name: R. L. Mazumdar v. Alfred Ernest
cases.principle: To support the conclusion that the appellant was a 'railway servant' as defined in the Indian Railways Act, against whom action could be taken under s. 138 of that Act, based on the terms of the agreements which gave the Railway administration extensive control over the appellant's work.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The protection of Article 311 of the Constitution is not available to a person who is not a member of a civil service as contemplated by the Article, nor has been dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank in a manner that would attract the protection of the Article.
obiter: The relationship of master and servant is characterised by agreement of service, express or implied, and whether or not a given agreement is one of service is a question of fact depending on its terms considered as a whole.

If a person's rights are confined to written agreements and they believe those agreements have been wrongfully terminated, they can challenge such termination in the civil courts and claim whatever relief is available to them under the law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that based on the extensive control the railway administration retained over the appellant's work under their agreements, he qualified as a 'railway servant' for the limited purposes of the Indian Railways Act, making him subject to summary proceedings under Section 138. However, this statutory classification did not elevate him to the status of a civil servant, and therefore he was not entitled to the constitutional protections against dismissal afforded by Article 311.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a person is a 'railway servant' under the Indian Railways Act, the court examines the terms of the agreement as a whole to see if the railway administration retains extensive power to direct, regulate, and control the manner of the work being done.

To determine if a master-servant relationship exists, the court looks for an 'agreement of service, express or implied,' which is a question of fact depending on the terms of the agreement considered as a whole.

To determine the applicability of Article 311 of the Constitution, the court applies a plain reading of the text to see if the person is a 'member of the civil service' and if the action taken constitutes being 'dismissed, removed or reduced in rank'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's claim that he was not a 'railway servant' failed because the court found the railway's retention of power to direct and regulate his work was sufficient to bring him within the definition of Sections 3(7) and 148(2) of the Indian Railways Act.

The appellant's claim for protection under Article 311 of the Constitution was rejected because a plain reading of the article showed he was not a member of the civil service, nor had he been dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank in the manner contemplated by that article.

The appellant's rights were found to be strictly confined to the written agreements, and any grievance regarding wrongful termination was a matter for the ordinary civil courts, not a defense against the summary proceedings under the Railways Act.
The Supreme Court found no legal infirmity in the orders of the High Court and the Sessions Judge that would justify interference under Article 136 of the Constitution.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the appellant was a 'railway servant' succeeded because the court agreed that the extensive control reserved by the railway administration in the agreements was the determinative factor. The court stated: 'The terms which govern the parties expressly reserve to the railway administration extensive power of directing and regulating the appellant's work and also, to an extent, of controlling the manner of doing the work.'

The respondent's position that the appellant was not entitled to Article 311 protection was upheld, as the court concluded that being a 'railway servant' for the purposes of the Act did not confer the status of a government civil servant.

The conclusions of the lower courts were affirmed, with the Supreme Court stating, 'we are unable to find any legal infirmity which would justify interference by this Court under Art. 136 of the Constitution.'
policy_considerations: The court reasoned that the railway administration's control over vendors like the appellant is a practical necessity for public service, stating: 'Keeping in view the purpose and object of these agreements, namely, that of affording necessary amenities to the travelling public, retention of this over• all power by the railway administration is not only appropriate but necessary.'
